label: Demo 1
title: Severe plaque psoriasis
symptoms: Severe plaque psoriasis on elbows, knees, and scalp. Failed clobetasol and UV light therapy.
transcript:
Dr. Vance: Good morning, Chloe. I’m Dr. Vance. Nice to meet you.

Chloe: Hi. Before we start — I’m recording this on my phone. I always mix up the medication names. Is that okay?

Dr. Vance: Yeah, that’s fine. Totally fine. So I was looking at your chart. You’ve been dealing with plaque psoriasis for a while. How’s it looking today?

Chloe: Honestly, it’s pretty bad. It’s on my elbows, my knees, my scalp. It cracks and bleeds when I bend my arms. I’d say it’s covering… maybe fifteen percent of my body?

Dr. Vance: I’m sorry. That sounds really painful. Are you still using the clobetasol your primary care doctor prescribed?

Chloe: Yeah. Twice a day, for like three months. And I did two months of the UV light therapy downtown. The light just dried me out. The ointment isn’t doing anything anymore.

Dr. Vance: Okay. Clobetasol is a strong topical steroid. Three months of that plus phototherapy, and it’s still this widespread — we’re past the conservative stuff. I want to start a biologic injection called Skyrizi. It targets the protein that’s driving the inflammation.

Chloe: I’ve seen the commercials. Isn’t that really expensive? My insurance fights me on everything.

Dr. Vance: They’ll want a prior authorization. That’s pretty standard for biologics. They usually want proof you tried cheaper things first. You’ve done high-potency topical steroids and phototherapy, and both failed. That’s the step therapy they look for. We’ll write the PA and attach your treatment history. My staff can start that today.

soap.subjective: 29F with long-standing plaque psoriasis. Reports plaques on elbows, knees, and scalp covering about 15% BSA; cracks and bleeds with motion. Used clobetasol BID for three months and completed two months of UV phototherapy without lasting improvement.
soap.objective: No new labs in this visit. Extent and failed topical plus phototherapy are from the patient’s report. [NEEDS VERIFICATION] body-surface estimate.
soap.assessment: Severe plaque psoriasis not controlled on high-potency topical steroid and phototherapy.
soap.plan_summary: Start Skyrizi (risankizumab); prior authorization likely. Document failed clobetasol and phototherapy. Follow up after the PA.

plan.notes: Step therapy documented: failed clobetasol and phototherapy. PA is not a paid claim.

plan.description: Continue clobetasol until the biologic is approved
plan.notes: Bridge only. Not a dose change.
Clinic submits the PA. CareLoop does not file it.

label: Demo 2
title: Low back pain with sciatica
symptoms: Lower back pain with sharp electrical pain down the right leg. Failed six weeks of PT and meloxicam.
transcript:
Dr. Aris: Morning, Sarah. It’s been about two months since we started the meloxicam and physical therapy. How are you holding up?

Sarah: Not great, honestly. PT helped a little at first. But the last three weeks I’ve had this sharp, electrical pain shooting down my right leg into my calf. I can barely sit at my desk. It’s waking me up at night.

Dr. Aris: I’m sorry. That’s new — the pain going down the leg. How many PT sessions did you actually get through?

Sarah: Twelve. Twice a week for six weeks, like you asked. And I’m still taking the meloxicam every morning. It barely takes the edge off. I even added Tylenol on top of it.

Dr. Aris: Okay. Pain shooting down the leg like that is often a pinched nerve — lumbar radiculopathy. You’ve done six weeks of PT and a prescription NSAID without much improvement, so we need a better look at the discs. I’m going to order an MRI of your lumbar spine, no contrast.

Sarah: Will insurance actually cover that? I know MRIs are expensive, and my plan denies everything.

Dr. Aris: They’ll probably flag it for prior authorization. A lot of plans want to see that you tried conservative care first. We’ve got that here — six weeks of PT, still on meloxicam, not better. That usually meets their step-therapy rules. My team can send the PA today with this visit note.

soap.subjective: 41F with ongoing low-back pain, now with three weeks of sharp electrical pain down the right leg into the calf. Completed 12 PT sessions over six weeks. Continues daily meloxicam; added OTC acetaminophen. Pain limits sitting and wakes her at night.
soap.objective: No imaging on file yet. Neurologic exam not documented in this transcript. [NEEDS VERIFICATION] strength, reflexes, and straight-leg raise.
soap.assessment: Lumbar radiculopathy suspected after failed conservative care. MRI indicated to evaluate discs. Not a diagnosis until imaging and clinician review.
soap.plan_summary: Order lumbar MRI without contrast; PA likely. Continue current conservative measures until imaging. Follow up on results.

plan.notes: Failed six weeks of PT and NSAID. PA is not a paid claim.
No dose change in this visit.
Clinic submits the imaging PA. CareLoop does not file it.

label: Demo 3
title: Chronic migraine
symptoms: Chronic migraine. Headaches most days, failed sumatriptan and Topamax.
transcript:
Dr. Thorne: Hi Elena, I’m Dr. Thorne. Welcome to neurology. I see your primary care doctor sent you over.

Elena: Hi. Really quickly — I’m using an app on my phone to record this. When I get a bad headache I get brain fog and forget everything. Is it okay if I leave it running?

Dr. Thorne: Yes. That’s a good idea, especially here. Leave it on. So the referral says severe headaches. Walk me through a typical month right now.

Elena: It’s a lot. Out of thirty days I probably have a headache on twenty of them. Ten or twelve turn into full migraines — nauseous, lights bother me, I have to sit in a dark room. I’m missing work.

Dr. Thorne: I’m sorry. That’s a heavy load. What have you already tried?

Elena: Sumatriptan when they start. It barely touches them now, and if I take it too often I get rebound headaches. Last year she put me on Topamax every day. I lasted four months. I felt like a zombie. Couldn’t concentrate, so I stopped.

Dr. Thorne: Yeah. Topamax does that for a lot of people. If you’re over fifteen headache days a month, that fits chronic migraine. The oral meds either aren’t working or the side effects were too much, so I want to talk about Botox injections. We do them here every twelve weeks.

Elena: I’ve read about that. My insurance is… not great. Are they going to fight me on it?

Dr. Thorne: They’ll want a prior authorization. Plans often treat Botox as cosmetic unless we show medical necessity. They look for step therapy — cheaper pills first. You’ve got the headache-day count, you failed an abortive with sumatriptan, and you couldn’t stay on Topamax. We’ll send the PA with that history today.

soap.subjective: 36F referred for headaches. About 20 headache days per month; 10–12 migraine days with nausea and photophobia. Sumatriptan now poorly effective; frequent use causes rebound. Trial of topiramate (Topamax) for four months stopped for cognitive side effects.
soap.objective: Neurologic exam not documented in this transcript. [NEEDS VERIFICATION] exam and headache diary if available.
soap.assessment: Chronic migraine by reported headache-day count after failed abortive and preventive orals. Botox is a next-step option pending clinician confirmation and PA.
soap.plan_summary: OnabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) every 12 weeks; PA required. Document failed sumatriptan and topiramate. Follow up after the first treatment cycle.

plan.notes: Failed sumatriptan and topiramate. Insurers may treat this as cosmetic without a PA. PA is not a paid claim.

plan.description: Continue sumatriptan as a rescue, limited days per month
Neurology follow-up after first Botox cycle
plan.notes: Clinic submits the PA. CareLoop does not file it.
